summary:
FireZone is a web platform designed to explore and understand wildfire-related thermal activity in Morocco. It combines historical NASA MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations into an interactive Burning Activity Calendar. Using a documented statistical harmonization method, it reduces differences between the sensors and helps users compare activity across years, identify seasonal patterns, and explore unusual periods.

The platform also provides a weather-based risk overview and a fire-spread simulator for exploring hypothetical scenarios. Users can view maps, download data, and review the methodology and evaluation results.

Developed as a student hackathon project, FireZone emphasizes transparency, reproducibility, and accessible scientific information. It supports research and awareness rather than providing confirmed fire predictions or operational emergency alerts.
details:
FireZone is a web platform that helps users explore historical burning activity in Morocco and understand the differences between satellite observations.

What does it do, and how does it work?
The platform uses NASA FIRMS data from MODIS and VIIRS. It groups observations into a common spatial and temporal framework, then applies statistical calibration to make their activity measures more comparable. An interactive calendar lets users explore monthly patterns and compare a selected month with its historical seasonal median. Additional features include a weather-based risk overview, hypothetical fire-spread simulations, and downloadable data.

What benefits does it have?
FireZone makes complex satellite records easier to understand. Users can explore multiple sources in one interface, investigate unusual activity, and review the methods behind the results. Harmonization helps reduce misleading comparisons caused by differences between sensors.

What is the intended impact?
The project aims to support environmental awareness, education, and research into Morocco’s fire activity. It provides a foundation for further collaboration with researchers and forest-management organizations. It is a research prototype, not a validated fire-prediction or emergency-warning system.

What tools and technologies did we use?

  • Frontend and server routes: Next.js, React, TypeScript, HTML, and CSS.
  • Data processing and evaluation: Python.
  • Maps: Leaflet, React-Leaflet, and MapLibre GL.
  • Data sources: NASA FIRMS, Open-Meteo, Copernicus DEM, and ESA WorldCover.
  • Simulation: PROPAGATOR, connected through a local Python service using FastAPI.
  • Development: Git, GitHub, npm, and local computers. No dedicated sensing hardware is required.

How is the project creative?
FireZone connects sensor harmonization with an accessible historical calendar, seasonal comparisons, and spatial exploration. Its contribution goes beyond displaying satellite points: it helps users interpret differences between datasets while keeping original observations separate from estimated indicators.

What factors did our team consider?
We considered sensor resolution, observation timing, confidence, missing coverage, product versions, and uncertainty. We separated calibration and evaluation periods, documented data provenance, and preserved reproducibility. We also considered mobile usability, clear visual explanations, limited student resources, and the importance of avoiding unsupported claims about prediction accuracy.
